tagline.text: A lone volcano rising from the Pangasinan plain, with a hot spring adventure resort

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–2,000 (per person for a day trip, depending on activities)

children.text: Mount Balungao is an isolated volcano rising about 382 m above the farmland of southeastern Pangasinan. You can swim and ride a zipline at the hot spring resort at its foot, then climb a steep forest trail in about an hour for a 360-degree view.
Mount Balungao rises about

above sea level as an isolated volcano in southeastern Pangasinan on Luzon, close to the Nueva Ecija border. The land around it is flat farmland, so its cone shape stands out clearly from far away. It is classified as a cinder cone, its last eruption is unknown, and the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) lists it as inactive. Tourism materials sometimes call it "extinct," but the official classification is inactive.
The mountain lies about
4–5 km

southeast of Balungao town center, and at its foot is the Balungao Hilltop Adventure, a hot spring resort built by the municipal government. The spring water is known to contain sulfur, and there are separate hot and cold pools so you can choose your temperature. Locals say the water is good for the skin, but no medical benefit has been confirmed, so think of it as a pleasant soak.
The appeal here is that you can do several things in one place. Climb lightly in the morning for the summit view, cool off in the spring pools afterward, and if you have time, try the
1.4 km

zipline or an ATV. The hike is manageable for beginners, but the slope is steep, so do not underestimate it. Few mountains in the Philippines stand alone in the middle of a plain, and from the top you can see at a glance how flat Pangasinan and Nueva Ecija are. Start easy, as you would on a small hill back home, but allow plenty of time for the tropical heat and humidity.
From Manila by bus and expressway it takes about
4–5 hours

, so a two-day trip combined with Manaoag Church or other Pangasinan sights works well. Prices and operations change from year to year, so check with the resort or the municipal tourism office before you go. It is also a convenient stop of a day on the way to Baguio or La Union, since it lies on the route from Manila to northern Luzon.

From the top, the plains of Pangasinan and Nueva Ecija spread out in every direction. On clear days you can see the ridge of the mountain range to the north and the town of Rosales to the west, and some visitors report a sea of clouds around noon. Rice fields and village roofs form a mosaic across the plain, which makes for good photos. Visibility drops on hazy days, so a clear morning is best. Reviewers also report seeing Mt. Amorong and Mt. Bangcay to the southeast, the Cuyapo area and Paitan Lake to the south, and the Cordillera ridge beyond the Caraballo range to the north-northeast.
The climb usually takes
45 minutes to 1.5 hours
and the descent
30 minutes to 1 hour

. Most of the trail is forested, with a grassland section near the summit, and you must use your hands on the rocky parts, so it suits beginners but still takes some fitness. The short grassland stretch at the edge of the forest near the top is the hottest and slipperiest part. A rope section is also installed, so go slowly and grip as you climb.

The resort at the foot has spring pools at different temperatures. They are ideal after a hike, and the upper pool may cost extra, so check when you enter. Night swimming runs separately from late afternoon and is listed at a slightly higher price than daytime.
The resort has a roughly
zipline and a roughly
1.4 km
zipline, plus a package that combines both. The 1.4 km line is billed locally as one of the longest in the country. Crossing the plain from a height is a thrill that appeals to adventure lovers.
ATVs are rented in
15 minutes
blocks, and there is also aero cable biking, where you ride a bicycle along an overhead cable. Availability changes with the season, so confirm on arrival.
Birds can be seen in the forest and rice fields around the mountain, and a birdwatching program is offered. Scopes can be rented and a guide can be arranged separately.
The resort has a steel suspension bridge linking the room building, gardens and pavilions. It is a good photo spot and one reason the resort is popular with families.
Take a tricycle or jeepney from Rosales Crossing to the resort. If you plan to hike, arriving early in the morning is best.
Pay the entrance fee at the resort and sign up for the environmental fee and a guide. Bring about 1.5 liters of water and gloves.
Start the hike with your guide. You pass through forest, rocky sections and the grassland near the top in turn.
Enjoy the view from the summit, take photos, then descend slowly.
Have lunch and relax in the hot spring pools to cool down.
Ride the zipline if you like. Visitors advise riding the zipline before going into the pool.
The red clay on the grassland section is very slippery after rain, so choose your shoes carefully.
Leave Manila for Rosales and drop your bags at the resort.
Climb the mountain or enjoy the hot springs and activities.
Rest in a resort room or a hotel in Rosales. Night swimming costs extra.
Visit Manaoag Church, then head home.
From Cubao in Manila, take a northbound bus such as Solid North, Victory Liner or Dagupan Bus toward Rosales. The trip takes about
4–5 hours
In a 2014 trip report the one-way fare was about
, so it may have risen since. Confirm at the terminal.
Get off at Rosales Crossing or SM Rosales.
Bus routes and fares change, so check the operator's latest notice before you leave.
Take NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX in turn and exit at Rosales. From there the resort is about
4 km
of uphill road.
Parking inside the resort is reported to be free.
From Clark Airport (CRK), the area is relatively close by car or rental car via TPLEX. I could not confirm a public transport connection, so check locally.
A special tricycle from Rosales Crossing costs about
, and because of the uphill road it usually carries only up to 3 people (based on past reports).
You can also take a jeepney to Balungao town hall or the market and switch to a tricycle. Reviewers say jeepneys from Rosales to Balungao Market run infrequently, so start early.
The dry season from November to May suits hiking. March and April bring shorter grass and a clearer trail, but midday is very hot.
In the rainy season the grass grows thick and the red clay is slippery and dangerous, so skip the hike and just enjoy the springs. Visitors note that Holy Week brings many families.
To avoid the midday sun, hike early in the morning. After the descent, resting in the spring pools is easier on the body.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Hike at dawn and soak in the afternoon; crowded in Holy Week
Slippery grass and clay sections; hiking not recommended

items.label: Resort entrance (daytime swimming)
items.note: Varies by year; discounts for children and seniors

items.label: Hiking guide
items.note: Per group of up to about 10 people

items.label: Room
items.note: For two people, breakfast reportedly included

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
The simplest place to stay is a room at the resort, listed in 2023 at about

for two with breakfast. Reserve ahead in peak season, and check the terms because the deposit may be non-refundable. For more choices, use hotels and lodgings in Rosales town. Check-in at the resort was listed as 1 p.m. and check-out at noon, so confirm that. Late check-out may cost extra.

For meals, use the resort's stalls or the restaurants in Rosales' shopping mall. Local snacks such as tupig and patupat and tuba are recommended, so give them a try. Outside caterers who are not residents reportedly pay a corkage fee of about
. Rosales has a large mall and fast food restaurants, handy when you miss Korean food or need to shop. Buying water and snacks before the hike is a good idea.
A guide is practically required for the hike. Arrange one at the resort, and call the town tourism office or the resort ahead of time to make it easier.
Bring gloves and long sleeves. Hands are easily cut on the grass and the sun is strong.
About 1.5 liters of water is reportedly enough, and you can refill at the starting point. On hot days, bring an electrolyte drink or salt candy too.
Ride the zipline before going into the pool.
Mobile signal from Smart is reportedly weak, so download your map beforehand.
Camping on the summit is reportedly prohibited, and camping is allowed only at the foot of the mountain.
The resort's operating schedule can change for maintenance, so call before you visit.
Local families crowd in on weekends and during Holy Week, so if you plan to hike, arrive early, climb first and use the springs in the afternoon for a more relaxed day.
Try to keep your bearings as you climb. On a clear day at the top, it is fun to find the surrounding mountains and towns on a map app.
After rain the red clay grassland is very slippery, so avoid hiking in the rainy season and climb with a guide.
The steep sections can be tough if your knees are weak or you are afraid of heights.
Some activities (ATV and zipline) may be suspended for maintenance, according to reviewers. If they are your goal, confirm in advance.
Prices differ between sources, so on-site prices may be different. Check the latest notice.
Shade is scarce at midday, so watch for heatstroke and drink plenty of water.
The benefits of the spring water are local belief and have not been confirmed medically. Take care if you have a skin condition or a chronic illness.
The road up to the resort is a steady climb, and tricycles usually carry only up to 3 people. If your group is large, decide on transport ahead of time.
It is about
1 hour
by car from the resort, so it pairs well as a combined trip. It is the largest pilgrimage site in Pangasinan.
The provincial capital of Pangasinan, where you can walk along the coast and see the capitol. It is far, so a separate day is recommended.
A riverside gorge park in Nueva Ecija and a nature destination in the same region. Check travel time locally.
The nearby town with SM Rosales, restaurants and transport links, useful as a supply and transfer base.
